name: Barban
lead: Two Defranceschi families in 1945, and the parish where the surname still appears in Croatian records today.
body: Acta Croatica records surviving Defranceschi households in the Labin area at Barban into the present century — one of only four Croatian places where the name is still found.

name: Cerovlje
lead: The municipality Gologorica sits in today.
body: Included here because modern Croatian administration files Gologorica under Cerovlje, so civil records after 1945 are found under this name rather than the village's own.

name: Gologorica
lead: The family's documented seat. A De Franceschi house of 1711 still stands on the main square.
body: Municipality of Cerovlje, central Istria. Roman material has been found here, including a gravestone now in the Pazin museum. The parish church of Saints Peter and Paul carries Renaissance altars and a seventeenth-century baptismal font, and a small Romanesque chapel of the Blessed Virgin keeps fifteenth-century frescoes.
Carlo De Franceschi, the historian, was born here in 1809 — of modest landowners, in his own biographer's phrase, not of gentry. In October 1945 the village still held two Defranceschi families.

registers.note: The six undigitised books are the oldest — baptisms 1644–1763, marriages 1656–1781, burials 1646–1777.

name: Gračišće
lead: Eight household censuses across 150 years — the richest register series found anywhere in this project.
body: First recorded in 1199. Held by the Patriarch of Aquileia, then the counts of Gorizia, and from 1374 part of the Duchy of Pazin. Bishop Paskazije of Pićan consecrated the Gothic chapel here in 1486, in his own birthplace.
Glagolitic and Latin graffiti survive scratched into the chapel interior — Croatian, written in Croatian letters, inside a town the maps called Gallignana.

registers.note: Thirty-one of thirty-two books digitised. The status animarum give house-by-house listings roughly every twenty years.

name: Ližnjan
lead: Named by the existing family research as the origin of a line that went to the United States and Germany — and never worked in an archive.
body: The received account gives Ližnjan as one of four directions the family dispersed in, onward to the United States and Germany. No register work has been done on it, and the 1945 census records no Defranceschi household here — which does not disprove the line, but does mean it had already gone by then.
Twenty-four registers survive, baptisms from 1683. Only fourteen are digitised, the lowest proportion of any parish in this study.

name: Motovun
lead: One family in 1945 — and 121 of 122 registers digitised, the most complete series in the study.
body: A Venetian hill town whose registers open in 1586. If a link has to be traced through the western, Venetian half of Istria, this is the easiest parish in which to do it.

name: Pazin
lead: The county town. Its baptism register opens in 1582 — the oldest book in this study.
body: Capital of the Habsburg County of Pazin from the late fourteenth century, and so the administrative centre for every village in this archive's Istrian half. Carlo De Franceschi sat for Pisino in the Imperial Constituent Parliament of 1848; his son Camillo attended the German gymnasium here.
One hundred and thirty-nine registers survive, but the 1643–1882 baptismal series is largely undigitised.

name: Pićan
lead: The diocese Gologorica and Gračišće belonged to — but not the custodian of their registers.
body: A tiny bishopric with an outsized place in Istrian church history; in the Middle Ages both ecclesiastical and secular power at Pićan lay with the Patriarchs of Aquileia. Its own registers run from 1664 and are almost entirely digitised. One Defranceschi family was counted here in 1945.

name: Poreč
lead: Where Camillo De Franceschi was born in 1868, and where his father published L'Istria in 1879.
body: The Gologorica branch reached Poreč before it reached Crikvenica. It is also the seat of the diocesan archive that holds the later registers for half the parishes in this study.

name: Seget
lead: An estate south of Umag, bought in 1720 by a de Franceschi family two generations out of Crete.
body: Venice granted the land in 1604 to families fleeing Greece and Montenegro. Captain Vincenzo Cuchich of Šibenik sold it in 1623 to the Venier of Venice, who held it a century and made it a working estate. In 1720 Nicolò and Marc'Antonio de Franceschi, sons of Giorgio, bought all of Catarina Bernardo Venier's Istrian property; in 1730 Umag made them citizens, them and their heirs.

They had reached Istria fleeing Crete after the Candian War of 1669. A monograph on the estate records that the family had two branches in Istria — one at Gologorica, one at Umag and Seget — and that family archives survive from both. One De Franceschi household was still counted at Seghetto in the 1945 census.

name: Svetvinčenat
lead: One De Franceschi family in 1945 — spaced, not fused — and a baptism register opening in 1568.
body: One of only two places in Istria in 1945 where the surname is written in the spaced Venetian form. The other is Seghetto near Umag. Both are west of the old Habsburg border.

name: Umag
lead: The hamlet of Seghetto held one De Franceschi family in 1945. Every one of Umag's 128 registers is digitised.
body: The only parish in this study with a complete digitisation — 128 of 128 books, marriages from 1602. Whatever is here can be read from anywhere.

name: Vižinada
lead: One family in 1945; registers from 1662.
body: In the Motovun judicial district and the Poreč administrative district in 1945 — the Venetian side of the peninsula.

name: Vodnjan
lead: Twelve Defranceschi families in 1945, and — since 9 September 2026 — five documented generations behind them. The best-attested cluster in southern Istria, read out of a register nobody has indexed.
body: The 1945 cadastre counts twelve Defranceschi families at Vodnjan, against two at Gologorica and one at Gračišće. For most of this archive's life that was all it knew, and the twelve households were listed as its second open question.

They are not open any more. The parish books of Dignano — FamilySearch catalogue item koha:963267 — hold baptisms from 1815, marriages 1815–1884 and deaths to 1893. The baptism register gives eight households between 1816 and 1865. **The marriage register has never been indexed by anybody**, and was read here opening by opening.

What came out of it: a line five generations deep, from a **Pietro** standing behind a marriage of the 1770s, through **Gio. Maria De Franceschi and Michiela Zambaletta**, to their children **Pietro, Cristoforo and Veniera** and the grandchildren married off in the 1820s. A **second, separate line** descending from a Domenico. **Four women of the name married out before the books open** — Domenica, Antonia Maria, Lucia and Veniera — recoverable only because their daughters' weddings named their mothers. And one household of three brothers, all «di Giuseppe»: **Don Stefano the priest**, who witnessed sixteen weddings under the parroco Giovanni Tromba, and **Pietro the ploughman and Cristoforo the weaver**, who signed the same book with a cross.

The town's church paperwork ran to the **Ordinariate of Pola**; the banns could be waived by the **Imperial-Royal Circle Captaincy**. Weddings involving Vodnjan people were also held at **Šišan** and **Svetvinčenat**, and a «Matt.o de Franceschi da Dignano» was buried at **Rovinj** in 1728 — the same formula, ninety-six years apart, naming the town only from outside it.

name: Čepić
lead: One family in 1945. The youngest register series in the study — nothing before 1782.
body: Recorded in the 1945 cadastre as Ceppici di Pòrtole, in the Motovun judicial district.

name: Crikvenica
lead: Named for a church: the Pauline monastery of 1412, in the deed that first records the name.
body: Nikola IV Frankopan gave the monastery to the Pauline fathers on 14 August 1412. The order stayed four hundred years, until Joseph II dissolved it in 1786, and for that whole time it was Vinodol's school, pharmacy and library.

A harbour came in 1877, a bathing beach in 1888, the first hotel in 1891 — a Vinodol village that became an Austrian seaside resort inside one lifetime. The Gologorica branch reached here by way of Poreč.

registers.note: Župa Crikvenica, 1798–1908, filmed from the Croatian State Archives. The register begins twelve years after Joseph II dissolved the Pauline monastery that gave the town its name.

name: Rijeka
lead: The largest documented concentration of the surname anywhere in Croatia — 447 records, once Vitipolis is recognised for what it is.
body: The indexed church books give 225 records under Fiume, 178 under Vitipolis and 44 under Rijeka. They are the same city. Vitipolis is the Latin for the city of Saint Vitus — Rijeka's patron, and the saint its cathedral is named for — which is also what the German Sankt Veit am Flaum means. Read together they make Rijeka the single biggest cluster of this family in the country, larger than Pola, Poreč and Omiš combined.

This is where the received account puts three separate arrivals: Domenico from 1614, Valentino out of Carnia made a citizen in 1739, and Giovanni Battista from the County of Pazin around 1740. The registers show de Franceschi children being baptised here from 1626.

registers.note: 447 indexed records under three names for one city.

name: Senj
lead: An Uskok garrison on the Habsburg Military Frontier — never Italian, unlike Istria.
body: Taken over by the Habsburgs in 1522 as a state-controlled Militärgrenze, and from the 1530s the base of the Uskoks, the refugee raiders who fought the Ottomans and Venice until an agreement between Habsburg and Venice expelled them in 1617. The Nehaj fortress was built by the Uskok captain Ivan Lenković in 1558.
Records for Senj fall to the State Archives in Rijeka, whose remit covers Primorje-Gorski Kotar plus the city of Senj. That inventory is not yet mapped.

registers.note: The Kvarner gap is now partly closed. FamilySearch holds microfilm of the Senj parish registers 1734–1920 and of Sv. Juraj near Senj 1695–1868, filmed from the Croatian State Archives in Zagreb — plus an Austrian army field-hospital register for 1805–06. The DARI collection itself still has no published parish-level inventory.

name: Mione
lead: A hundred and thirty people at 710 metres — and the Italian end of a documented migration into Istria.
body: First written on 15 June 1185, when Odolrico called Gusetto, Strabo, and Vecellone, son-in-law of Giovanni da Mione, received concessions from Domenico, abbot of Moggio. An independent comune until 1871, now a frazione of Ovaro in the Canale di Gorto.

A stone above the village, at some 1,600 metres, carries Venetic inscriptions — this valley was a route long before it was a parish. From the parishes of Ovaro and Luincis a long series of weavers took the road into Istria; the documents become numerous in the seventeenth century and frequent in the eighteenth.

registers.note: Confirmed dead end: FamilySearch holds only the Napoleonic civil registration for Ovaro's frazioni — Mione, Luincis, Luìnt, Muina, Ovasta, Liariis, Entrampo, Lenzone, Agrons e Cella, Cludinico, Muscletto, Chialina — filmed from the Archivio di Stato di Udine. There are no Ovaro parish books on film anywhere online. The pre-1806 church registers must be asked for at the parish.

name: Imotski
lead: Taken from the Ottomans in July 1717 with a De Franceschi first over the wall. The family has been here three hundred years.
body: Of the seventy Venetians living at Imotski after 1717, only the de Franceschi settled permanently in the Imotska krajina. They held the Perinuša estate — the former begluk of arci-beg Čaušević, with land, houses, a mill and a tower on the Vrljika — and they are still present, physically and in the town's memory, though most of the arable land and the mills are gone and many members have scattered.

There is a long local antagonism to go with it: a persistent belief that the liberation was owed solely to the Imotski Franciscans and the people, which casts the acquisition of Perinuša as a seizure. The estate had in fact been Ottoman crown land, held by begs; who owned it before that is lost in medieval darkness.
Fewer than five people named Franceschi live at Imotski today.

held: FamilySearch film, from HDA Zagreb and Zadar
registers.note: The Podjezerja book runs 1693–1733 and so spans the siege of 1717 itself; Imotski-Glavina picks up in 1731. Both were filmed from the Croatian State Archives.

name: Omiš
lead: A former pirate town at the Cetina mouth, and the Dalmatian family's first seat — a De Franceschi owned a warship here by 1590.
body: The de Franceschi are said to have reached Dalmatia in the fourteenth century as an influential Italian noble house, and to have established themselves at Omiš, where Gaspar de Franceschi is recorded in 1590 as owner of the warship Vascello and later admiral of the fleet.

Zuane Ivan Franceschi sat on the town council here, and it was as an Omiš councillor that he pressed the Imotski refugees' case with the Venetian Provveditore Generale. His estate at Dobrč — today Pisak, along the coast — is where he sheltered them from January 1715.

registers.note: Župa Omiš, 1588–1894. The series opens two years before Gaspar de Franceschi is recorded here as owner of the warship Vascello, which makes this the one place where the Dalmatian family's earliest claim can actually be tested.

name: Split
lead: Twenty-five Franceschi — the largest single concentration of any spelling of this name anywhere in Croatia.
body: Acta Croatica records about sixty people named Franceschi in Croatia today, in thirty households, against fifty in the middle of the last century — an increase of twenty per cent. They are Croats, from Split, and most were born at Split or Imotski.

This is the mirror image of the Istrian story. The Defranceschi of the Pazin area have fallen from about fifty mid-century to about ten; the Franceski of Rijeka from thirty to a single household. Only the Dalmatian branch is growing.

name: Rovinj
lead: The town that holds this archive's earliest dated Istrian record, and the church where Carlo De Franceschi was married at his own bedside.
body: Two of the three oldest De Franceschi records this archive has in Istria are Rovinj burials of men who did not live here. **«Adì 27 Mago 1619 · morì ser Piero di Franceschi da Pola»** — carried into the town to be buried, with an offering of 24 lire on a page whose other entries run at 2, 6 and 12. And on 27 December **1728**, **«Ob.to di Matt.o de Franceschi da Dignano»**. A book of burial offerings catches whoever dies in the parish, which is why a register here names men of Pula and of Vodnjan.

The film also holds a Rovinj household across three generations — Giacomo → Vittorio, who married Domenica Moscarda → Piero Anto, baptised 1736 — and a Bona Defranceschi, daughter of Dominicus and Oliva Dorligurro, marrying in the 1840s: that is the Vodnjan household sending a daughter here.

And on **1 March 1852**, entry 31: **Carlo De Franceschi**, the historian, «Assessore presso quest'I. R. Corte di Giustizia», married Maria Michelcich **«al letto dello Sposo, per essere gravemente ammalato»** — at the bridegroom's bed, gravely ill, on banns dispensed that same day by the Imperial-Royal District Captaincy. He lived another forty-one years. Two years later the same film records the burial of «Julius, son of Carlo», born 1853, dead 13 February 1854.

name: Pula
lead: The see and the port at the foot of Istria — and the town a De Franceschi is called «da Pola» from, in 1619.
body: Carlo's own *L'Istria* lists Franceschi among the noble families of Pola «venuti da Capodistria» before the plague of 1631 — which makes Pula one of the two candidate parents for the southern Istrian clusters, the other being Koper itself.
The earliest dated record this archive holds in Istria names a man of this town rather than of the one he was buried in: **«ser Piero di Franceschi da Pola»**, buried at Rovinj on 27 May 1619.

Pula is also where the church paperwork of the whole south ran. The marriage dispensations entered in the Vodnjan register are issued by the **Ordinariate of Pola** — «dell'Ordinariato di Pola» — and that is the office to write to for what those registers only allude to.

name: Kaštelir
lead: A hilltop village under Vižinada, and the reason a wrong answer about Vodnjan looked convincing for an hour.
body: The one death this archive found on film 005497893 — **Mathaeus De Franceschi, son of Antonius, house 32, died 7 August 1819** — sits in the *Liber Defunctorum of Castellier*, that is Kaštelir, which is kept under **Vižinada**.

That is precisely why the film's catalogue entry answers «Župa Vižinada» and why this archive briefly concluded that all seventy-eight Vodnjan records were really Vižinada's. **A reel can carry more than one parish**, and this one carries Vižinada's deaths and Vodnjan's baptisms. The correction is on the Vodnjan page; the village that caused it deserves its own.

name: Bakar
lead: The deep-water bay east of Rijeka, and one of the Kvarner parishes where the surname sits in the registers with no line yet attached to it.
body: Bakar belongs with Rijeka and Ledenice in the group of Kvarner parishes this archive can name people in but cannot yet join to any line. The households here are treated as **unplaced** — documented, and honestly unattached — rather than folded into the Carnia or Pazin-county descent on the strength of a shared surname.

name: Draguč
lead: A walled village north of Cerovlje with twenty-five indexed records of the name — and not one of them read yet.
body: Twenty-five records carrying this surname are indexed at Draguč. **They are on this archive's queue and have not been opened.** It is listed here so that the gap is visible rather than silently absent: an indexed record left unread is a different thing from a register that no index reaches, and both are counted separately in the Search Register.

name: Premantura
lead: The last village before the cape at the bottom of Istria, and one of the southern parishes the surname holds in.
body: Premantura sits with Ližnjan, Fažana, Šišan and Vodnjan in the southern Istrian group. The households here are documented in the sweeps but not yet worked through a register page by page, which is the only method that has produced generations in this part of Istria.

name: Fažana
lead: The fishing village opposite Brijuni, north of Pula, with reconstructed households of the name.
body: Three households of the surname were reconstructed here from indexed records. Fažana belongs to the same southern cluster as Vodnjan and Premantura, and like them it has never been read register-page by register-page — which, at Vodnjan, is what turned twelve households in a 1945 cadastre into five documented generations.

name: Telve
lead: In the Valsugana, east of Trento — the largest single concentration of the name outside Istria and Dalmatia in this archive's roster.
body: Twenty-two people of the surname in this archive sit at Telve, more than at any Istrian village except Vodnjan. They come out of David's family tree rather than out of a register this archive has read, and **no descent connects them to the Istrian or Carnian families**. Defranceschi is a common Trentino surname formed independently from the same patronymic; that is the working assumption here and it is an assumption, not a finding.
Telve is listed so the twenty-two are visible and counted, not folded into a line they may have nothing to do with.

name: Laives
lead: South of Bolzano in the Adige valley — a second Tyrolean cluster, and like Telve unattached to any Istrian line.
body: Eleven people of the name, from the family tree rather than from a register read here. Laives belongs with Telve, Strigno and Fiera di Primiero in the Trentino–South Tyrol group: same surname, different formation, **no documented connection to Istria**.

name: Strigno
lead: A Valsugana village a few kilometres from Telve, with the same surname and the same open question.
body: Grouped with Telve and Fiera di Primiero. Counted here rather than absorbed into an Istrian line.

name: Torrington
lead: A brass town in the Naugatuck valley of Connecticut, and the largest American landing-place in this archive.
body: Twelve people of the name in Torrington. The New England brass and clock towns took Istrian and Trentino labour in the same decades that Brooklyn took the Gallignana families, and this is where a cluster of them settled.
Nothing here has yet been checked against a federal census or a naturalisation file. **That is the next step for this place**, and it is the method that worked for the Eleven in Brooklyn.

name: Pfullingen
lead: Below the Swabian Alb, near Reutlingen — where the German leg of David's own line came to rest after 1947.
body: Anton Rudolf Defranceski appears on the Pfullingen list of foreigners in 1947 and was certified by that town's mayor in 1950. Pfullingen, Reutlingen, Neuhausen an der Erms, Metzingen and Bad Urach are one small district, and the family's German years happen inside it.
This is the leg of the journey that a walking itinerary is still owed for.

name: Postira
lead: On the north shore of Brač, with three reconstructed households of the name.
body: Postira sits with Omiš and Split in the Dalmatian group. Three households here were reconstructed from indexed records; none has been read register-page by register-page.

name: Santa Maria di Sala
lead: In the Veneto between Padua and Venice — a mainland Venetian parish carrying the name.
body: Six people, from the tree rather than from a register read here. Relevant because the Venetian line of this archive — the printers, the Grand Chancellor, the Omiš and Zadar families — is a Venetian-state story, and mainland parishes of the Republic are where its ordinary people would be.

name: Šterna
lead: A hamlet in the Buje hinterland, north-west Istria, with a documented household of the name.
body: Šterna appears in the eighteen-town sweep and on the journey map. Its households are listed as **unplaced**: documented, and honestly unattached to any line.

name: Vrsar
lead: The bishop of Poreč's own port, south of the Lim channel.
body: Three people of the name. Vrsar was the temporal lordship of the bishops of Poreč until 1778, which puts it in the same ecclesiastical world as Gologorica under the bishops of Pedena — the family farmed a bishop's rent there.

name: Plomin
lead: Above its bay on the eastern Istrian coast, at the Kvarner end of the county of Pazin.
body: Three people of the name. Plomin sits on the road between the Pazin county villages and the Kvarner shore — the same route the Carnia line is inferred to have taken to Fiume.

name: Paluzza
lead: In the Val But of Carnia, on the road to the Plöcken pass — one of the valleys the 1679 headmen's list covers.
body: Paluzza belongs with Mione, Ovaro, Muina and Givigliana in the Carnian group. The documented link to Istria is the 1679 list on which a Zuane De Franceschi of Mione is recorded working in the County of Pazin with his son; Paluzza is on the map because the walking itinerary crosses it, not because a person of the name is yet documented here.
